newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat candidate sees Swiss solution for Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Croat candidate sees Swiss solution for Bosnia.

text.p: For Kresimir Zubak, elected as the Croat member of Bosnia's new collective presidency, the only solution for the divided state is to create a Switzerland in the Balkans.

While Bosnians of all factions can only dream of Swiss-style peace and prosperity, Zubak believes the Swiss model giving a lot of power to local communities and strictly limiting the role of central government might just work.
Zubak, a 49-year-old ex-judge, applies this solution to the Moslem-Croat federation, a U.S.-arranged marriage between two of Bosnia's three factions of which he is president.
But. as member of the collective presidency, he will have to consider the model for saving the whole nation from disintegration.

"If the federation is indeed the political concept of both nations -- the Bosnian Moslems and the Croats -- its chances are very good," said Zubak, a relative moderate in a Bosnian political scene often dominated by hardline nationalists.

"If we play an honest game, there is enough room for complete affirmation of both nations in the social, economic, political and cultural spheres, enough room for free life and free development," he said earlier this year.
"This could be a prosperous community, like similar communities in the world such as Switzerland."
Zubak was born in the northern Bosnian town of Doboj, now controlled by the Serbs.

Despite his reputation as a moderate, his credentials as a patriotic Croat are strong. Serbs destroyed his family home when the war began in 1992 and in the same year he was wounded while fighting for the HVO, the Bosnian Croat militia.
He also pugnaciously defends Croat interests in the federation, which is still not functioning properly.

"The main problem lies with the other side," he said recently. Zubak blamed reluctance by the Moslem-led Bosnian government in Sarajevo to disband its "Agency for Information and Documentation" which he calls a secret police.
He says he has good communication with the federation's top Moslem representative, Vice President Ejup Ganic, and with Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic.
But he warns the Moslems that they must respect the Swiss model, where different communities co-exist with large decentralised powers -- or face the consequences.
"The greater the tendency towards centralisation in Sarajevo, the greater the aspiration for secession among the Croat people," he said.
Zubak is married to a Serb. Mixed marriages were common in pre-war Yugoslavia, however, and this does not in itself guarantee his reputation as a moderate.

He offered his resignation as federation president after last year's U.S.-brokered Dayton peace agreement because he was frozen out of the negotiations. But he quickly withdrew it and supports the concept of a multi-ethnic presidency.
"If there had been any better solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would never have accepted the Dayton accords," he said.
He believes Bosnia has a 50-50 chance of survival although Serb leaders want to secede. "Perhaps peaceful co-existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina will take root again," he said.
"Perhaps they will see that it is possible for us to live together ... and that other people's traditions and customs do not endanger their national security and culture."
